The Swiss position is the more defensible one.  
Denial of the Holocaust is not an abstract historical debate; it is a deliberate vehicle for anti‑Semitic hatred, a denial of genocide, and a threat to the dignity of its victims. Treating such denial as a criminal offense aligns with a broader goal of protecting human rights, combating discrimination, and upholding the memory of those who suffered. By contrast, treating it as protected speech in the United States prioritizes a very broad conception of free expression but does little to counter the hate‑motivated intent behind the denial, leaving victims and vulnerable communities unprotected. From a normative standpoint—balancing freedom of speech with the imperative to safeguard fundamental human dignity and prevent incitement to hatred—criminalizing Holocaust denial is consistent with European anti‑discrimination norms and the broader duty to protect against hate‑based extremism.
